ta-l1d37q2-d1e97.summary: The Prooemium to Quaestio 2, stating that the question now turns to how God is said to be everywhere (ubique), and identifying the three articles to follow: whether God is everywhere; whether this belongs to God alone; and whether it belongs to him from eternity.

ta-l1d37q2-d1e109.summary: First objection of Article 1. To be everywhere signifies being in every place. But Anselm says that, if usage permitted, God should rather be called 'with every place' than 'in every place.' It seems, therefore, improper to say that God is everywhere.
claims: Anselm's preferred locution ('with every place' rather than 'in every place') suggests 'God is everywhere' is not strictly proper speech.

ta-l1d37q2-d1e112.summary: Second objection. Just as time names a certain measure, so does place. Per the Philosopher, to be in time is to be measured by some part of time; so to be in place signifies being measured by place. But God is immense (unmeasurable). Therefore God is not in place.
claims: Being in place, like being in time, implies being measured by it; since God is immense and unmeasurable, he cannot be in place.

ta-l1d37q2-d1e115.summary: Third objection, from Anselm's authority: whatever is in place and time follows the laws of place and time — implying this would be unfitting to affirm of God.
claims: Anselm holds that whatever is in place and time is subject to the laws of place and time, which seemingly cannot apply to God.

ta-l1d37q2-d1e119.summary: Fourth objection. As successive things relate to time, so permanent things relate to place. But in successive things, a single indivisible entity or operation cannot exist at diverse times. Therefore a single indivisible permanent thing cannot exist in diverse places either. Since God is indivisible, he cannot be everywhere.
claims: By analogy with the impossibility of one indivisible successive act occurring at multiple times, one indivisible permanent thing (God) cannot exist in multiple places at once.

ta-l1d37q2-d1e122.summary: Fifth objection. No corporeal condition can belong to God except metaphorically. Being in place is a condition of natural body, so much so that (per the Philosopher) even metaphorical bodies are given place only by way of likeness. Much more, then, does being in place or being everywhere belong to God only metaphorically.
claims: Since being in place is a corporeal condition, it can be attributed to God only metaphorically, as with other corporeal conditions.

ta-l1d37q2-d1e125.summary: Sed contra: God is in all things, as was established in the preceding article. But any place is itself some thing. Therefore God is in every place, and hence everywhere.
claims: Since God is in all things and place is itself a thing, God is in every place, i.e. everywhere.

ta-l1d37q2-d1e128.summary: The main determination (respondeo) of Article 1. Being-in-something belongs differently to spiritual and corporeal things: a body is in something as contained (as wine is in a vessel), while a spiritual substance is in something as containing and conserving it. The reason is that a corporeal thing, by its essence circumscribed by the limits of quantity, is determined to a place, so that its power and operation are in that place; but a spiritual substance, wholly free from position and quantity, has an essence not wholly circumscribed by place, and so is in place only through its operation — and consequently its power and essence are also there. Thomas concludes: if 'being in this place' is taken as body is said to be in place, it belongs to God to be everywhere only metaphorically, since he fills place not by dimensional extension but by the causality of his effects. But if 'being in place' is taken as a spiritual substance is said to be in something, then it belongs to God most properly to be in place and everywhere — not as measured by place, but as giving to place its very nature of locating and containing, just as God is said to be in man insofar as he gives man the nature of humanity, and is said to be in any thing insofar as he gives things their proper esse and nature.
claims: A body is in place as contained; a spiritual substance is in place as containing and conserving.
Because a spiritual substance is free from quantity and position, it is in place only through operation, and hence its power and essence are also present there.

God is 'in place' or 'everywhere' properly (not metaphorically) only when 'being in place' is understood in the mode proper to spiritual substances — as giving place its nature of locating, not as measured by it.

ta-l1d37q2-d1e131.summary: A single reply covering the first, second, and fifth objections together with the objection from Anselm's authority, noting that all of them proceed according to the mode in which a body, rather than a spiritual substance, is said to be in place — a mode already shown in the respondeo not to be the sense in which God is properly said to be everywhere.
claims: Objections 1, 2, 5, and the Anselm-authority objection all wrongly assume the corporeal mode of being-in-place, which the respondeo has already distinguished from the proper, spiritual mode applicable to God.

ta-l1d37q2-d1e134.summary: Reply to the fourth objection. 'Indivisible with respect to succession' is said in two ways: either that which is wholly free from succession (negatively indivisible), like eternity, which — because its unvarying 'now' is present to every part of time — can exist at diverse times, indeed at every time; or that which is the terminus of succession, like an instant, which cannot exist at several times. Likewise 'indivisible with respect to dimension' is said in two ways: either that which is wholly free from dimension, like a spiritual substance, for which it is not incongruous to be in many or all places; or that which is the terminus of dimension, like a point, which, being fixed to a position, cannot be in several places. Thomas concludes that, setting imagination aside, the indivisibility of an incorporeal substance — God, an angel, the soul, or even matter — must not be conceived on the model of the indivisibility of a point, since, as Boethius says, one must not be led back to imagination in intellectual matters.
claims: Eternity's negative indivisibility (freedom from succession) allows presence at every time, unlike the instant's indivisibility as terminus of succession.
Similarly, a spiritual substance's dimensional indivisibility (freedom from quantity) allows presence in many places, unlike a point's indivisibility as terminus of dimension.
The indivisibility proper to incorporeal substances must not be modeled imaginatively on the indivisibility of a geometrical point.
concepts: warning against imagination in intellectual matters

ta-l1d37q2-d1e146.summary: First objection of Article 2. It is heretical to hold that prime matter is God, or even that universal being is God, as some have held. But (per the Philosopher) the universal is everywhere and always, and likewise prime matter, which is in every body and by which every place is filled, since nothing is void. It seems, therefore, that being everywhere does not belong to God alone.
claims: Since the universal and prime matter are also everywhere and always, being everywhere cannot be exclusive to God.
concepts: heresy of identifying matter/universal with God

ta-l1d37q2-d1e149.summary: Second objection. In all numbered things there is some number. But all the parts of the universe are numbered. Therefore the collected number is in the whole universe, and so is everywhere.
claims: Number, as present in every numbered part of the universe, would likewise be everywhere, challenging the exclusivity of divine omnipresence.

ta-l1d37q2-d1e152.summary: Third objection. Per Augustine, the whole soul is in each part of the body it animates. But God could have created only a single animated body. In that case its soul would be everywhere [in that one body/universe]. Yet what belongs to God alone is communicated to no creature. Therefore being everywhere does not belong to God alone.
claims: If God had created only one animated body, the soul's Augustinian wholeness-in-every-part would make the soul 'everywhere' too, threatening the exclusivity of divine omnipresence.
concepts: Augustine on the soul's presence in the body

ta-l1d37q2-d1e156.summary: Sed contra: Ambrose in the text proves that the Holy Spirit is God because he is everywhere. But this proof would carry no force unless being everywhere belonged to God alone. Therefore being everywhere belongs to God alone.
claims: Ambrose's argument for the divinity of the Holy Spirit from his omnipresence presupposes that omnipresence is exclusive to God.
concepts: omnipresence as a mark of divinity

ta-l1d37q2-d1e159.summary: The main determination (respondeo) of Article 2. Being everywhere, taken per se, belongs to God alone and cannot be communicated to any creature; but it can belong to something per accidens. This accidental sense can arise in two ways: from the side of the thing that is in place, or from the side of place itself. From the side of the thing: since what is attributed to a whole by reason of its part belongs to it only per accidens or per posterius, whatever is in diverse places according to its diverse parts is not primarily and per se in all of them, but is per se in one place only; so even an infinite body would be everywhere only per accidens (insofar as its parts are everywhere), not per se. From the side of place: something can happen to be 'everywhere' merely because no other place exists besides the one it occupies — as if only one place existed, containing one man — but this would fail were other places to exist. God alone is everywhere per se: he is wholly present in any given place, and would be present in all of them even if infinitely many other places existed; and this cannot be communicated to any creature unless a being of infinite power were communicated to it.
claims: Being everywhere per se belongs to God alone; created things can be called 'everywhere' only per accidens.
Per accidens omnipresence arises either from a whole being distributed across parts occupying different places, or merely from the absence of any other place to be in.
God's per se omnipresence — being wholly present in any place, however many places might exist — presupposes infinite power and so cannot be communicated to a creature.
concepts: per se vs. per accidens omnipresence

ta-l1d37q2-d1e162.summary: This passage resolves all three objections at once: everything cited in them (the universal, prime matter, the hypothetical single body's soul, number) is 'everywhere' only per accidens — either because it is distributed according to diverse parts, or because no other places happen to exist, or because it does not exist by a single act of esse in the several places where it is found (as with the universal and with things that exist in diverse places according to different instances of esse). Number itself is not per se in place at all, yet insofar as it is in place, it is not wholly in one place but distributed across diverse places according to its diverse parts.
claims: The universal, prime matter, and a hypothetical world-soul are 'everywhere' only per accidens, unlike God's per se omnipresence.
Number is not per se in place, and when considered as in place, it too is distributed according to parts rather than wholly present in each place.

ta-l1d37q2-d1e174.summary: First objection of Article 3. It seems that being everywhere belongs to God from eternity, first because Ambrose states in the text that God is in all things and everywhere always, which is proper to divinity; and what is always, is eternal. Therefore being everywhere belongs to God from eternity.
claims: Ambrose's statement that God is everywhere always, taken as a mark of divinity, seems to entail that omnipresence belongs to God from eternity.

ta-l1d37q2-d1e177.summary: Second objection. Just as 'everywhere' distributes place, so 'always' distributes time. But God is always, from eternity, even when times do not exist. Therefore he is also everywhere from eternity, even when places do not exist.
claims: By analogy between 'everywhere' (distributing place) and 'always' (distributing time), God's eternal 'alwaysness' should imply an eternal 'everywhereness,' even prior to the existence of places.

ta-l1d37q2-d1e180.summary: Third objection. God's being in things is here coordinated by the Master (Peter Lombard) with things being in God. But things were in God from eternity, since he has eternal knowledge of them. Therefore God is also in things, and everywhere, from eternity.
claims: The parallel Lombard draws between 'God in things' and 'things in God,' combined with the eternity of divine knowledge, seems to entail that God's presence in things is likewise eternal.
concepts: things in God via divine knowledge

ta-l1d37q2-d1e184.summary: Sed contra: wherever something is, that thing must exist, since in nothing, nothing at all exists. But neither place nor any thing existed from eternity. Therefore it does not belong to God to be everywhere, or in things, from eternity.
claims: Since neither place nor creatures existed from eternity, God's being 'in' them cannot itself be an eternal state of affairs.

ta-l1d37q2-d1e187.summary: The main determination (respondeo) of Article 3. To say 'God is everywhere' implies a certain relation of God to creature, founded on some operation through which God is said to be in things. But every relation founded on an operation proceeding into creatures is predicated of God only temporally (ex tempore) — like 'lord' and 'creator' — because such relations are actual and require both of their extremes actually to exist. Therefore, just as God is not said to operate in things from eternity, neither is he said to be in things from eternity, since this designates his operation.
claims: 'God is everywhere/in things' expresses a relation founded on divine operation toward creatures.
Relations founded on operation into creatures (like 'lord,' 'creator,' 'in things') hold of God only temporally, since actual relations require both terms to actually exist.
Since God's operating in things is not eternal, neither is his being in things.
concepts: temporal (ex tempore) predication of relational names
lord and creator as analogous cases

ta-l1d37q2-d1e190.summary: Reply to the first objection. Ambrose means that God is always everywhere given that creatures exist: what is on God's own side is always, containing nothing new, but the defect lies on the side of the creature, which has not always existed; hence God's being everywhere cannot be signified as an eternal relation to creatures, i.e. as operating with respect to them from eternity.
claims: Ambrose's 'always everywhere' presupposes existing creatures; the eternity is on God's side, while the temporal limitation belongs to the creature, so the relational statement is not itself eternal.

ta-l1d37q2-d1e193.summary: Reply to the second objection. 'Always,' strictly speaking, signifies a certain indefectibility, which eternity possesses wholly and at once, while time obtains it through the succession of its parts; hence 'always' can signify the indefectibility achieved through continuous succession — in which sense it distributes times and does not belong to God from eternity, since succession and time did not themselves exist from eternity — or it can signify the indefectibility of eternity itself, in which sense it does belong to God from eternity. But 'everywhere,' in its very notion, includes place; so the two cases are not parallel, since wherever there is being-in-place, 'everywhere' requires being in every actual place.
claims: 'Always' is ambiguous between the indefectibility of temporal succession (not eternal) and the indefectibility of eternity itself (eternal).
'Everywhere' has no analogous eternal sense, because it conceptually presupposes the actual existence of places, unlike 'always' with respect to eternity.
concepts: conceptual dependence of 'ubique' on actual places

ta-l1d37q2-d1e196.summary: Reply to the third objection. Just as motion takes its character from its terminus, so does relation. When it is said that God is in things, a relation of God to creatures is implied according to the outgoing (egressus) of divine operation into them — and since creatures are not eternal, neither can being-in-them be eternal. But when it is said that things are in God, a relation of creature to God is implied not according to an exit from him but rather according to the union of creatures to their principle; and because that principle is eternal, the knowing is likewise eternal, and things are in God from eternity. Thomas concludes: God is in things temporally, according to the mode of things, but things are in God from eternity, according to the mode of God — because whatever is in another is in it according to the mode of that in which it is, not according to its own mode.
claims: 'God in things' and 'things in God' are not symmetrical relations: the former follows the temporal egress of divine operation, the latter the eternal union of creatures to their principle in divine knowledge.
The general principle 'whatever is in another is there according to the mode of the container, not of itself' explains why things can be eternally in God even though God is only temporally in things.
concepts: relation takes its species from its terminus

ta-l1d37q2-d1e206.summary: The Expositio textus glosses four separate phrases from the base text with short interpretive comments. (1) On 'God, though wholly and essentially in all things, is more fully in those he indwells': other creatures, though they follow the divine likeness through God's own operation, do not attain to God himself according to supposit (person); so although God is in them, they are not 'with' God. But the rational creature, through grace, attains to God himself insofar as it loves and knows him, and so is said to be 'with' him, called 'capable of God' as its perfecting object, and for this reason called the temple of God and indwelt by God. (2) On the asymmetry between what we understand of God but cannot express, and what we say of God but cannot understand: since a cause always exceeds its effect, in matters learned through instruction (e.g. purely revealed truths, 'faith is from hearing,' Rom. 10) speech causes understanding, and the learner's understanding may not reach the full power of the words heard, so one can speak what one does not fully understand; but in matters known through discovery, understanding is the cause of speech, and so understanding exceeds speech, such that much is understood that cannot be put into words. (3) On the denial that the divine essence is properly in every place: some erred here by taking 'being in place' in the corporeal mode, and so denied God's essence is properly in place, saying instead he is there 'through essence' only insofar as every essence derives from him and insofar as he operates through the power of his own essence — but this is insufficient without what was established in the preceding article (that God is properly present as containing, not contained). (4) On the question of how God is substantially present in all things without being affected by them: this question is called foolish, since not everything that touches must be changed by what it touches — mutual alteration occurs only between things that act and are acted upon by sharing matter (per De Generatione I), as the sphere of the moon is unaffected by contiguous fire; so it is foolish to say the divine essence is polluted by the unclean things to which it applies itself through operation.
claims: Non-rational creatures are indwelt by God but are not 'with' God, since they attain only a likeness of God through his operation, not God himself; rational creatures, through grace of love and knowledge, attain God himself and so are called God's temple.
Speech can outstrip understanding (in matters of faith learned by hearing) or understanding can outstrip speech (in matters discovered by reason), because a cause always exceeds its effect.

God's presence in place is properly that of the containing spiritual substance, not merely that every essence derives causally from him — a point requiring the fuller account given in the preceding article.
Touching does not entail mutual alteration except between things sharing matter, so the divine essence's contact with impure things through operation does not defile it.
concepts: corporeal vs. spiritual mode of place

ta-l1d37q2-Dd1e92.summary: The Prooemium to Quaestio 2, consisting of a single paragraph that identifies the three articles to be pursued: whether God is everywhere, whether this belongs to God alone, and whether it belongs to him from eternity.

ta-l1d37q2-Dd1e101.summary: Article 1 asks whether God is everywhere. Five objections argue against a proper sense of divine omnipresence: Anselm's preference for 'with every place'; the implication that being-in-place entails being measured by place, incompatible with divine immensity; Anselm's principle that whatever is in place and time follows their laws; the impossibility, by analogy with successive things, of one indivisible permanent being existing in diverse places; and the merely metaphorical applicability of corporeal conditions like place to God. The sed contra infers God's omnipresence directly from his universal presence in all things established in the prior quaestio. In the respondeo, Thomas distinguishes the corporeal mode of being-in-place (as contained, like wine in a vessel) from the spiritual mode (as containing and conserving), and concludes that God is 'everywhere' only metaphorically if the corporeal sense is meant, but most properly and literally if the spiritual sense is meant — since God gives place itself its very nature of locating, just as he gives every thing its proper esse and nature. The replies dismiss objections 1, 2, 3, and 5 as trading on the corporeal sense of place, and resolve objection 4 by distinguishing an indivisibility that is merely the terminus of succession or dimension (which cannot be multiply present) from an indivisibility that is wholly free of succession or dimension (like eternity or spiritual substance), which can be present at every time or in every place, warning against modeling the latter on the imaginative picture of a geometrical point.
claims: God is 'everywhere' only metaphorically if 'in place' is understood in the corporeal sense (as contained), but properly and literally if understood in the spiritual sense (as containing and giving place its nature).

The indivisibility proper to spiritual substances and to eternity differs in kind from the indivisibility of a point or an instant, and it is this former kind that permits multiple, simultaneous presence.
concepts: corporeal vs. spiritual mode of place

ta-l1d37q2-Dd1e138.summary: Article 2 asks whether being everywhere belongs to God alone. Three objections propose apparent counterexamples: the universal and prime matter, said by the Philosopher to be everywhere and always; number, present in every numbered part of the universe; and, hypothetically, a single world-soul that (per Augustine's principle that the whole soul is in every part) would be everywhere in a single-bodied universe. The sed contra appeals to Ambrose's proof of the Holy Spirit's divinity from his omnipresence, which presupposes that omnipresence is God's alone. In the respondeo, Thomas distinguishes omnipresence per se, belonging to God alone as an implication of infinite power, from omnipresence per accidens, which can arise either because a whole is distributed across parts occupying different places, or merely because no other place happens to exist. The replies show that every counterexample in the objections — the universal, prime matter, the hypothetical world-soul, and number — instantiates only the per accidens sense, never God's unique per se, whole-in-every-place mode of omnipresence.
claims: Being everywhere per se, as being wholly present in every place regardless of how many places might exist, belongs to God alone and presupposes infinite power.

All apparent counterexamples (universal, matter, a hypothetical world-soul, number) achieve omnipresence only per accidens, either through distribution of parts or through the mere absence of other places.
concepts: per se vs. per accidens omnipresence

ta-l1d37q2-Dd1e166.summary: Article 3 asks whether being everywhere belongs to God from eternity. Three objections argue for an eternal omnipresence, appealing to Ambrose's description of God as always everywhere, to the parallel between the distributive terms 'always' and 'everywhere,' and to Lombard's coordination of 'God in things' with the eternity of things being known in God. The sed contra counters that since neither place nor any thing existed from eternity, God's being in them or everywhere cannot itself be eternal. In the respondeo, Thomas argues that 'God is everywhere/in things' expresses a relation founded on divine operation toward creatures, and such relations — unlike God's absolute attributes — hold only temporally (ex tempore), since they require both relational terms actually to exist, just as 'lord' and 'creator' do. The replies clarify Ambrose's 'always' as conditional on creatures' existence rather than asserting an eternal relation; distinguish an 'always' that signifies temporal indefectibility (not eternal) from one that signifies eternity's own indefectibility (eternal), while noting 'everywhere' has no parallel eternal sense because it conceptually presupposes actual places; and explain, via the principle that relation takes its character from its terminus, why 'God in things' is only temporal (following the temporal egress of operation) while 'things in God' can be eternal (following the eternal union of creatures to their principle in divine knowledge), since whatever is in another exists there according to the mode of the container, not of itself.
claims: Because 'God is everywhere/in things' expresses a relation founded on divine operation toward creatures, and such operational relations require both terms to actually exist, this relation — unlike God's own eternal being — holds only temporally, not from eternity.

'Things in God' can nonetheless be eternal, since that relation follows the eternal union of creatures to their principle in divine knowledge rather than the temporal egress of operation into them; each relation is measured by the mode of what contains it.

ta-l1d37q2-Dd1e201.summary: The Expositio textus, a single paragraph glossing four separate phrases of the base text: why God, though wholly present in all things, is said to be 'more fully' in those he indwells (because only the rational creature, through grace, attains God himself rather than a mere likeness of him); why understanding and speech about God can each outstrip the other (because a cause always exceeds its effect, differently in matters learned by instruction versus matters discovered by reason); why the claim that God's essence is not 'properly' in every place is insufficient on its own (because it rests on the corporeal, rather than the spiritual-containing, mode of place already corrected in the preceding articles); and why the question of how God is substantially in all things without being defiled by them is foolish (because contact entails mutual alteration only between things sharing matter, not between the divine essence and what it touches through operation).
claims: Only the rational creature, through grace, attains God himself rather than a mere likeness, which explains why it alone is called God's temple and is 'with' God.

The commentary's four glosses each correct or clarify a point already established in the body of the quaestio (spiritual vs. corporeal presence, the asymmetry of language and understanding, and non-alteration through contact).

ta-l1d37q2.summary: Quaestio 2 of Distinction 37 investigates how God is said to be everywhere (ubique), following the prior quaestio's establishment that God is in all things. It divides into a Prooemium and three articles, followed by an Expositio textus glossing the base text. Article 1 shows that God is properly, not merely metaphorically, everywhere when 'being in place' is understood in the spiritual mode of containing and conserving rather than the corporeal mode of being contained, since God gives to place itself its very nature of locating. Article 2 shows that this per se omnipresence — being wholly present in any and every place, however many places might exist — belongs to God alone, since it presupposes infinite power, whereas every apparent creaturely counterexample (the universal, prime matter, a hypothetical world-soul, number) achieves ubiquity only per accidens. Article 3 shows that this omnipresence, precisely because it expresses a relation founded on God's operation toward creatures, holds only temporally rather than from eternity — unlike the converse relation of things being eternally in God through his eternal knowledge, since each relation takes its mode from the reality that contains it. The Expositio textus then clarifies, via four brief glosses, why only rational creatures are said to be fully indwelt by and 'with' God, why speech and understanding of God can each exceed the other, and why God's substantial presence in all things, including unclean things, does not defile him.
claims: God is everywhere properly (not metaphorically) in the spiritual sense of containing and giving place its nature, this omnipresence belongs to God alone because it presupposes infinite power, and it holds only temporally rather than from eternity because it is a relation founded on operation toward creatures.
Only the rational creature, through grace, attains God himself rather than a mere likeness, and is therefore alone said to be indwelt 'with' God as his temple.
concepts: per se vs. per accidens omnipresence
